entries.text: In the mud by the landing stone there are no small clawed prints at all, only the long print with the bite out of the third line, twice since yesterday's: one pointed at the forest, a fresher one pointed at the water. Whoever it is crossed over to my side again and went back.

entries.text: Across the water the gray shape hangs still on its poles and nobody is at the plank table. The slosh was right where that one's light goes down to the water. I think the one in goggles wades.

entries.text: Lifted the flat stone off the first sack and scooped two handfuls into the bindle. Seven days in the pool now; the water off them runs clear and the meats bend without breaking.
entries.title: Seven days soaked

entries.text: Roasted them a few at a time on the stick over this morning's coals and ate them hot on my heels by the ring. No bitter at all, and now my stomach is quiet.

entries.text: The first thing I asked only brought back animal tracks and stone ones from long ago. The second found it: a print with no toes and lines across the bottom is a sole, something worn on the foot, and every sole's pattern and wear are its own, so the bite is that one foot's mark.
entries.title: A print with lines

entries.text: So whoever crosses the stones wears something on its feet, and it is always the same something. My feet only ever leave my feet.

entries.text: Picked every meat off the low shelf into the bindle. The sun is coming through the round window in patches between clouds, so they go out to the drying stone.

entries.text: Spread the meats one layer deep on the drying stone. The clouds closed over before I finished, so there is no sun on the stone, only the breeze coming off the water and moving over them.

entries.text: Drew the long print on the thirty-sixth page as near as I can remember it: no toes, lines straight across, and the bite out of the third line. Wrote 'same foot, always' under it.

entries.text: It says nothing about clouds. Soaked meats dry one layer deep in low warmth with air moving past, turned every hour, and take about twelve hours; the sky today hasn't got twelve hours of sun in it.

entries.text: So the stone was only half of it. They get turned every hour, and if the sun stays away they go on the warm side of the ring, out of the smoke.

entries.text: Knelt at the pool to drink and something moved under my face: small fish, finger long, holding still in the shade behind the ring stones, all pointed at where the creek comes in. My hand went in and every one was gone; they came back slowly, one at a time.

entries.text: Across the water the one in goggles sat on a box by its plank table, bent over something in its lap that gave off a little light, the way my slate does. It never looked up, and I didn't wave.

entries.text: It only told me about one small fish, one that lives in ditches and ponds eating mosquito larvae and other insects. Nothing about my pool, but small fish eat small things that move.

entries.text: So they hold facing upstream for whatever the creek brings down to them. I go to the basket every morning for whatever comes, and mostly it's leaves.

entries.text: Roasted six of the drying meats on a stick over the coals and ate them hot. The smoke kept leaning off to the northwest in the gusts, and leaves kept coming down into the ring.
entries.title: Warm acorns

entries.text: Lifted a stone from the edge of the pool and turned it over. Stuck to the underside were little flat crawlers no bigger than a fingernail, six legs spread wide and two thread tails, and they ran sideways to stay under it.
entries.title: Under a stone

entries.text: Flicked one crawler onto the pool. Before it sank halfway the nearest fish had it and was back behind its stone. Leaves have been landing on the water all morning and not one fish went up for a leaf.
entries.title: Before it sank

entries.text: The first thing I asked found it. You tie a thorn to the line by its blunt end and push the point into a fat grub, so thorn and line make a V; when a fish takes it you let it run and wait about half a minute before pulling, so it has swallowed it.
entries.title: A thorn by its end

entries.text: So the trick isn't quick hands, it's slow ones: thirty breaths of letting go. The brambles have more thorns than I could ever use.
entries.title: Slow hands

entries.reason: He was hungry and the fire was still up.
entries.text: Ate a double handful of the meats from the bark tray, warm from the ring and a little chewy. I want my hands steady for the next part.
entries.title: Lunch from the tray

entries.reason: He needed thorns for the hook the slate described.
entries.text: Snapped thorns off the gray dead canes, since the green ones bend instead of break. The longest is barely a fingernail; the page said a whole thumb joint. The fish in my pool are only a finger long, so maybe that's right.
entries.title: Dead canes

entries.reason: To have something real to try on the fish.
entries.text: Tied a thorn onto nettle cord by its blunt end. The knot slid off twice; the third time I wound it four turns and pinned it with a second knot, and now it hangs in a V like the page said.
entries.title: A V of cord

entries.reason: He needed bait for the thorn hook.
entries.text: Turned the same edge stone over and picked off one crawler, the fattest. It held on to my finger with all six legs, which is more grip than I had expected.
entries.title: One for the thorn

entries.text: Upstream across the water the one in goggles was crouched in its shallows. It jerked a line up out of the creek, looked at the end of it, and sat back on its heels. The line came up shorter than it went in.
entries.title: A short line

entries.reason: He wanted to try his first hook the slow way.
entries.text: Pushed the thorn into the crawler and let it down. A fish took it and ran under the ring stones, and I let it go and counted thirty breaths like the slate said. When I pulled, the cord came up light: crawler gone, fish gone, and the tip of the thorn snapped off.
entries.title: Thirty breaths

entries.reason: His hands were slow and cold from the pool.
entries.text: The fire was down to embers when I got back. Laid dry sticks on and blew until it stood up, and held my hands over it; pool water stays in the fingers a long time.

queries: thorn fish hook snapped what else can i make a hook from in the woods
entries.query: thorn fish hook snapped what else can i make a hook from in the woods
entries.reason: His thorn snapped off in a fish's mouth and he wanted something stronger.

entries.text: It never says thorns snap, which mine did. It says hooks have been made of bone, claws, teeth and hard wood, and that a little gut hook can be whittled from oak, sharp at both ends, so it sticks crosswise once it's swallowed. I have an oak and I have a knife.
entries.title: Hard wood, both ends

entries.reason: The slate said hard wood, and oak is the hardest I know.
entries.text: Picked through the leaves under my red oak for a dead twig, not a green one; the dead ones snap clean and the green ones only fold. Found one a finger thick and gray all through. The wind kept dropping more leaves on my back while I looked.
entries.title: A dead oak twig

entries.reason: To make a hook that won't snap off in a fish like the thorn.
entries.text: Whittled a sliver off the oak twig and took it down by the fire, sharp at both ends with a groove round the middle for the cord. Oak fights the knife; a birch pen is butter next to it. It came out about as long as my smallest finger's top joint.
entries.title: Harder than birch

entries.text: Upstream across the water the one in goggles was crouched in its shallows, washing something in the water that flashed silver when it turned. Whatever it was, it was about as long as one of my fish.
entries.title: Something silver

entries.reason: He wanted to see if oak would hold where the thorn snapped.
entries.text: Wound the crawler onto the oak hook and let it down. The fish came and tugged at it from both ends, round and round, and stripped the crawler off without ever taking the hook in. When I pulled it up, the oak was bare and whole.
entries.title: Picked from both ends

entries.text: The oak didn't snap, but my fish are only a finger long, and the hook is half the length of their heads. It needs to be a splinter, not a peg. My fingers are cold and slow from the water again.
entries.title: Too fat for them

entries.reason: His hands were too cold and slow from the pool to whittle anything thin.
entries.text: Laid three dry sticks across the flames and sat close with my hands open over the heat. The fingers came back one at a time, the little ones last.
entries.title: Three sticks

One page says the old ones were bamboo with the cord tied off center, so one end is longer and stands up crosswise when pulled, and the bait is pushed along the whole length so none of it shows. Mine was tied in the middle with the crawler wound round it like a bandage.

entries.reason: The slate said one end should be longer than the other.
entries.text: Split a much thinner sliver off the oak twig and took it down until it bends a little, about as thin as a pine needle. Cut the groove a third of the way along instead of the middle, so one end is long.
entries.title: Thin as a needle

entries.reason: To see if a thin splinter does what the fat peg couldn't.
entries.text: Slid the crawler along the whole splinter so no oak showed and let it down. A fish swallowed it and I counted thirty, and when I drew in it was heavy and came up flashing right to the ring stones, then twisted once and was gone. The splinter came back whole.
entries.title: Right to the stones

entries.text: It held long enough to come up, which nothing has before. Next time I lift it straight out onto the bank instead of drawing it to the stones where it can twist. My fingers are cold again.
entries.title: Closer than ever

entries.reason: Last time he drew the fish to the stones and it twisted free.
entries.text: Hid the splinter in a crawler again and counted thirty after the cord went tight. Then I didn't draw it in, I lifted, and a speckled fish a little longer than my finger came up out of the water and landed flapping in the leaves behind me.
entries.title: Out onto the bank

entries.text: I sat down on the bank and held it in both hands until it stopped. All day for one fish the size of a finger, and I'd do the whole day again.
entries.title: My first fish

entries.text: Not always: some little fish get eaten whole. But the guts make the meat spoil fast and slow the heat from reaching the middle, and the belly can hold whatever the fish swallowed. Mine is going on a stick over coals, so the insides come out.

entries.reason: The slate said the insides slow the cooking.
entries.text: Slit its belly with my little knife and washed it out in the pool. The guts sank, and the other fish came straight out from behind the stones and took them.

entries.reason: He was hungry, and he wanted to know what his own fish tasted like.
entries.text: Roasted it on a stick until the skin went brown and curled, and ate it in four bites, little bones and all. It tastes like the pool smells, only warm. Not a meal yet, but it's the first food I ever pulled out of the water.

entries.reason: So the way it worked doesn't get lost by tomorrow.
entries.text: Wrote the first fish on the thirty-seventh page: the splinter hidden in a crawler, count thirty after the cord goes tight, then lift, don't draw. Drew it a little longer than it was, then crossed that out and drew it right.

entries.reason: He wanted a second fish so supper would be more than four bites.
entries.text: Turned over four stones at the edge of the pool before one had a crawler under it. The light is going gray and the water is colder on my hands than it was at noon.

entries.reason: Lifting worked once and he wanted to see it work twice.
entries.text: Counted thirty and lifted, and nothing came with it but the splinter, clean. Something took the whole crawler off without ever pulling. One fish today, then.

entries.text: Across the water a small yellow light came on at the plank table of the one in goggles, about the same time as last night. It stayed bent over the table and never looked out.

entries.reason: He was cold from the pool and wants coals for supper.
entries.text: The fire was down to red embers, so I laid dry sticks on them and blew until they caught. My fingers were slow on the sticks until the heat got into them.

entries.reason: One fish was four bites, and the meats have been drying all day.
entries.text: Took a handful of meats from the bark tray, dry on top and still leathery underneath, and held them over the coals on a stick until they ticked and browned.

entries.reason: He wanted to be full before the cold part of the night.
